Proof of Work · Prompt Engineering

Same AI. Same task.
A better prompt changes everything.

This page is not a claim — it is a demonstration. Below are four real tasks, each shown three ways: the weak prompt most people type, the engineered prompt I would actually write, and the output that prompt produces. Judge the skill by the work.

01RoleWho the AI should act as — an expert with a point of view, not a generic assistant.
02ContextThe situation, the audience and the facts the answer has to respect.
03ConstraintsLength, tone, what to avoid — the guardrails that stop generic filler.
04FormatThe exact structure of the answer: sections, table, bullets, word count.
05ExamplesA sample of the target quality, so "good" is defined, not guessed.

Example 01 / Product Copy

Etsy product description for a spreadsheet template

The product: a Home Bakery Pricing Calculator (Excel + Google Sheets) that works out the true cost per cake — ingredients, time, packaging and overhead — and suggests a profitable selling price.

The weak prompt

"Write a product description for my cake pricing spreadsheet."

Why it fails: no audience, no benefits, no structure. The AI guesses — and guesses sound like every other listing: "easy to use", "save time", "perfect for bakers". Nothing a buyer can act on.

The engineered prompt 
ROLE: You are an Etsy copywriter who specialises in digital
products for home-based food businesses.

PRODUCT: "Home Bakery Pricing Calculator" — an Excel and
Google Sheets workbook. The baker enters ingredient costs,
batch size, time spent, packaging and overhead; it calculates
the true cost per cake and a selling price at their chosen
profit margin. Includes a price list tab and an order tracker.

AUDIENCE: Home bakers selling from Instagram and WhatsApp
who currently price by guessing or copying competitors.

WRITE: An Etsy listing description with this structure:
1. A one-line hook naming the pricing problem (max 15 words)
2. "What it does" — 4 bullets, each starting with a verb,
   each tied to a money outcome, not a feature
3. "What's inside" — list the tabs
4. "Who it's for / not for" — 2 lines each, be honest
5. Requirements line (Excel or Google Sheets, instant download)

CONSTRAINTS: Under 220 words total. No hype words
("revolutionary", "game-changer", "must-have"). No income
guarantees. Friendly, plain English a non-native speaker
reads easily. Use "you" throughout.
The output

Stop guessing your cake prices — know exactly what each one costs you.

What it does

  • Calculates your true cost per cake — ingredients, your time, packaging and overhead included
  • Shows the selling price you need for the profit margin you choose
  • Flags the recipes that are quietly losing you money
  • Tracks every order and payment in one place, so nothing gets forgotten

What's inside: Pricing Calculator · Ingredient Cost Library · Price List · Order Tracker · Simple dashboard

Who it's for: home bakers who sell regularly and price by feel. Not for: bakeries with POS software, or anyone wanting a recipe book — this is a numbers tool.

Requirements: Microsoft Excel or a free Google account for Google Sheets. Instant download, works on Windows, Mac and phone.

What changed: the weak prompt produces adjectives; the engineered prompt produces a buying decision — a named problem, money outcomes, honest limits, and a format a skimming buyer can scan in 20 seconds.

Example 02 / Business Email

A polite but firm late-payment follow-up

The situation every freelancer knows: an invoice 14 days overdue, a good client relationship worth protecting, and a payment that still needs to arrive this week.

The weak prompt

"Write an email asking my client to pay my invoice."

Why it fails: the AI doesn't know the amount, the dates, or the relationship — so it writes something either apologetic and weak ("sorry to bother you…") or cold and threatening. Both damage the freelancer.

The engineered prompt 
ROLE: You are a professional freelancer writing to a
valued client. Your tone: warm, confident, zero apology
for asking — this is business, handled gracefully.

FACTS:
- Client: Sarah, owner of a small marketing studio
- Work delivered: social media template pack, delivered
  and approved on 28 September
- Invoice: #INV-014, $350, due 6 October — now 14 days overdue
- One friendly reminder already sent on 9 October, no reply
- Goal: payment this week, relationship fully intact,
  door open for the next project

WRITE: An email of 120–150 words:
1. Subject line — factual, includes the invoice number
2. Open with the delivered work, positively, one line
3. State the fact plainly: invoice number, amount, due date
4. Make paying effortless: "reply to this email and I'll
   resend the payment link"
5. One gentle consequence, framed as process not threat:
   new work pauses until open invoices are cleared
6. Close warmly, referencing future work together

CONSTRAINTS: No "just checking in", no "sorry", no
exclamation marks, no legal language. Short paragraphs.
The output

Subject: Invoice #INV-014 — $350, due 6 October

Hi Sarah,

Glad the template pack landed well with your team — it was a pleasure putting it together.

I'm writing about invoice #INV-014 for $350, which was due on 6 October and is still open. It may simply have slipped through, so I've kept this short: reply to this email and I'll resend the payment link right away.

One housekeeping note — I schedule new projects once open invoices are cleared, so settling this week keeps us on track for the November work we discussed.

Thank you, and speak soon.

Best regards,
Areeb

What changed: every fact the email needs was supplied, so nothing is vague. The "consequence" is framed as scheduling policy, not a threat — firm on the money, warm on the relationship.

Example 03 / Content Planning

A week of LinkedIn ideas for a cleaning business

The owner of a small cleaning company wants LinkedIn visibility with local businesses — offices, clinics, property managers — not generic "content". One post a day, Monday to Friday.

The weak prompt

"Give me LinkedIn post ideas for a cleaning company."

Why it fails: no audience, no goal, no formats. The result is motivational filler — "Monday motivation!", "meet our team!" — that no office manager has ever hired a cleaner from.

The engineered prompt 
ROLE: You are a B2B content strategist for local
service businesses.

BUSINESS: BrightNest Cleaning — 6-person team cleaning
offices, dental clinics and rental properties in one city.
Owner posts personally, 15 minutes a day maximum.

AUDIENCE & GOAL: Office managers, clinic owners and
letting agents on LinkedIn. Goal is enquiries, not likes.
Every idea must either prove competence, show a real
cost of dirty workplaces, or teach one useful thing.

WRITE: 5 post ideas, Monday to Friday, as a table:
Day | Hook (the exact first line, under 12 words) |
Format (text / photo / 30-sec video / poll) | The post in
2 sentences | Soft call to action

RULES:
- Rotate formats: no two days the same
- At least one idea uses a real number or a before/after
- At least one is a story about a specific job (no client
  names)
- No motivational quotes, no "happy Monday", no hashtag
  lists inside the hooks
- Ideas must be filmable/writable in 15 minutes
The output
DayHookFormatThe postCTA
Mon"Your office kitchen is costing you staff."TextA short breakdown of a real survey stat: shared kitchens are the #1 complaint in office feedback — and the cheapest one to fix."When did yours last get a deep clean?"
Tue"This clinic reception took 40 minutes to reset."Before/after photoTwo photos from a permitted job, one line on what a patient-ready reception actually involves behind the scenes."Clinics: we do out-of-hours. DM for a walkthrough."
Wed"We lost a contract in March. Here's why."Text storyAn honest story: a client left over missed bins — and the checklist system the team built so it never happens again."What would make you fire your cleaner?"
Thu"What does office cleaning actually cost per desk?"30-sec videoOwner on camera, one number explained: cost per desk per month, and what changes the price up or down."Want the number for your office size? Comment the headcount."
Fri"Property managers: your 24-hour turnover checklist"Poll + checklistA 6-item end-of-tenancy checklist as a text post, ending with a poll: which item gets missed most often?"Save this for your next move-out."

What changed: each idea now has a buyer, a proof point and a reply path. "Content" became a quiet sales system the owner can run in 15 minutes a day.

Example 04 / Operations

Messy meeting notes → a clean action list

Raw notes from a 30-minute call about a website redesign — half-sentences, names, dates and decisions all mixed together. The team needs tasks, owners and deadlines, nothing else.

The weak prompt

"Summarise these meeting notes."

Why it fails: a summary repeats the mess in nicer sentences. Nobody can work from it — owners are implied, deadlines stay buried in prose, and decisions blur into discussion.

The engineered prompt 
ROLE: You are an operations assistant who turns raw
notes into task lists a team can execute without questions.

INPUT: The meeting notes pasted below this prompt.

WRITE exactly three sections, in this order:
1. DECISIONS — bullet list, only things clearly decided,
   one line each. If it was discussed but not decided,
   it does not belong here.
2. ACTIONS — a table: Task | Owner | Deadline.
   Task starts with a verb. Take the owner and date from
   the notes exactly as written. If no date is given,
   write "— not set" instead of inventing one.
3. OPEN QUESTIONS — anything mentioned but unresolved,
   phrased as a question, with who should answer it.

CONSTRAINTS:
- Use ONLY facts from the notes. Never invent a date,
  name, number or decision.
- If a note is ambiguous, put it in Open Questions —
  do not guess.
- No introduction, no conclusion, no commentary.
  The three sections only.
The output

Sample input (the messy notes): "call w/ danish + priya — homepage redesign, launch before diwali sale. danish said hero section new banner needed, he'll design by fri. priya: product pages loading slow, needs dev help, ask areeb?? budget approved 40k for photoshoot — decided. checkout page complaints — tabled, decide next week. priya to send brand files to danish today. sale dates not final, marketing to confirm. danish — mobile menu broken on android, fix urgent."

DECISIONS

  • Homepage redesign to launch before the Diwali sale
  • Photoshoot budget of 40,000 approved
  • Checkout page discussion postponed to next week

ACTIONS

TaskOwnerDeadline
Design new hero bannerDanishFriday
Send brand files to DanishPriyaToday
Fix broken mobile menu on AndroidDanish— not set (marked urgent)
Investigate slow product-page loadingPriya— not set

OPEN QUESTIONS

  • Who will handle the dev work for the slow product pages — Priya flagged "ask Areeb?" but it wasn't confirmed
  • What are the final Diwali sale dates? (Marketing to confirm)
  • What is the deadline for the Android menu fix, given it's marked urgent?

What changed: the constraint "never invent a date" is the whole game. The AI flagged the unconfirmed owner instead of silently assigning the task — an output the team can trust without re-reading the raw notes.

The Difference

What changes with an engineered prompt

01Specificity

Real facts go in — amounts, dates, names, audience — so real answers come out. A weak prompt forces the AI to guess, and guesses are what make AI writing sound like AI writing.

02Format control

The answer arrives in the shape you need: a scannable listing, a 140-word email, a table, a three-section task list. No re-editing a wall of text into something usable.

03Tone on purpose

"Polite but firm", "warm, zero apology", "no hype words" — tone is specified like a setting, not hoped for. The same task can produce five different voices, each deliberate.

04Reusable as a system

An engineered prompt is an asset. Save it, and next month's invoice chase, listing or meeting notes take two minutes — same quality, every time. That is the difference between a trick and a workflow.
